column4: The section makes night a cover and daylight an opening, then moves from what is hidden to what is said. This verse puts concealed speech and public speech beside someone hidden by night and conspicuous by day, showing that both sides of the image are known to God.

The source section says words reach people by hearing or revelation and describes what is covered. This verse says that even speech made aloud leaves a secret and what is still more hidden, setting a limit on what public telling can expose.

The section describes blessings as both apparent and hidden. This verse applies the paired terms to God as the Manifest and the Hidden, shifting the visible/hidden distinction from the gift to its giver.

The section’s closing command concerns the favor of the Lord. This verse states that every blessing people have is from Allah, making explicit the attribution that the section asks its reader to voice.

The section moves from night and day to telling the Lord’s favor. This verse joins night and day with giving both secretly and publicly, a concrete parallel between hidden and open acts of generosity.
The verse describes punishment reaching towns at night or while their people rest at midday. It places the section’s two covered and exposed times in one scene of unexpected disclosure.
The verse asks whether a town feels secure from punishment arriving at night while its people sleep. It gives the hidden, sleeping side of the section’s night/day contrast.
The next verse asks whether a town feels secure from punishment arriving at duha while its people play. It supplies the exposed daylight counterpart to the sleeping night in 7:97.
The verse describes dawn being split, night as repose, and the sun and moon as measures. It makes the cover-to-day transition a created order, not just a shift in visibility.

The verse says God covers day with night as it pursues it, and names the sun, moon, and stars as subject to command. This repeats the section’s covering image in a larger account of the alternation of night and day.
The verse asks whether people see that night was made for rest and day for sight. It repeats the section’s contrast between what is hidden in night and what becomes visible by day.
The section calls night a covering beneath which things are unseen. These youths are made to sleep in a cave for years, a specific concealment that precedes their awakening.

The next verse says God awakens them so they may learn which group can best estimate how long they remained. It completes the concealment with a return to awareness and an attempt to name what passed unseen.

The section joins the night cover, exposure to the sun, and being guided or lost. This verse describes the sun turning away from the cave’s people and ends by distinguishing whom God guides from whom He leaves astray.
The youths seem awake though they are sleeping, and their dog lies at the cave entrance. This is a specific difference between what sight suggests and what remains hidden within the cave.

The youths awaken, ask one another how long they have remained, and send one to the city for food while urging discretion. It joins finding provision with the need to keep their hidden state from being exposed.
The youths fear being discovered and forced back into their former religion. This completes their concealment scene by naming what exposure would mean for them.

The source section’s dictionary gloss calls a town’s outward side its exposed edge. A man runs from the far end of Moses’s city with a warning, a specific scene of a voice emerging from the city’s edge into public view.

The source section’s dictionary gloss describes the exposed side of a town; the connection here is spatial rather than lexical. A man comes running from the farthest part of the city to urge his people to follow the messengers, so the city edge becomes the point from which a public message emerges.
The section describes وَجَدَ as noticing through perception. Moses finds two women holding their flock back from the watering crowd, notices their need, and asks what is happening.
After Moses waters their flock, he withdraws to shade and asks his Lord for whatever good He sends. The continuation connects a found need and a response with asking for provision.

A woman comes to Moses with her father’s invitation and the offer of a reward for watering the flock. The good deed that began with noticing need is made known through a spoken message and returned provision.

The section imagines someone hidden in a crowd and found at a glance. This verse describes needy people who appear self-sufficient but are recognized by their marks, making concealed need perceptible without an insistent request.
The section’s surrounding surah says not to rebuff the asker. This verse states that a due share of wealth belongs to the asker and the deprived, turning hidden generosity into an explicit right.
The verse says that the faithful keep a known share in their wealth, a detail that makes provision answerable to people in need rather than remaining solely with its holder.
The next verse identifies the recipients as the asker and the deprived, directly connecting the section’s treatment of a petitioner with a claim on provision.

The section describes finding by the senses and reason and moving from concealment to what is exposed. In Joseph’s story, his master is found at the door after a hidden encounter, and the woman’s torn shirt becomes visible evidence.
The verse introduces a witness who says to inspect which side of Joseph’s shirt is torn. It supplies the reasoning test that can turn a concealed event into a known one.
The witness says a tear from behind would show the woman’s accusation is false. This verse gives the physical criterion by which the hidden event can be judged.
The master sees the shirt torn from behind and recognizes the deception. This completes the passage from hidden action to evidence found and then interpreted.

The section uses water disappearing into milk as an image of something present but unseen within another substance. This verse describes pure milk emerging from within the animal, a related but distinct image of a drink whose origin lies hidden inside.

The section labels ض ل ل branch B004 with the dictionary sense “forget.” Moses asks not to be taken to task for what he forgot, a direct example of memory failing in the same narrative as the lost fish.
The section connects disappearance with forgetting and gives 2:282 as its example. This prayer asks not to be held accountable if people forget or err, making forgetfulness a named human limit.
The section’s secondary sense of ض ل ل is forgetting. This verse says Adam had previously been given a command but forgot it, showing a forgotten instruction rather than a lost path.

The section cites deniers who ask how people can be created anew after disappearing into the earth. This verse stages a person’s death for a century and return to life, with his food and drink preserved and his donkey restored, as a concrete answer to that denial.

The section reports denial of resurrection after bodily disappearance. Abraham asks how God gives life to the dead, and is shown birds gathered back after being placed on separate hills, a specific reversal of disintegration.
The verse repeats the question whether people will be raised in a new creation after becoming bones and fragments, another formulation of the section’s cited denial after disappearance.
The verse asks whether people will be raised after dying and becoming dust and bones. It repeats the same bodily-disappearance challenge as the section’s 32:10 passage.
The verse asks whether people will be resurrected after they die and become dust and bones, a further direct formulation of the denial the section quotes.
The verse quotes people asking whether they will be resurrected after dying and becoming dust and bones. It repeats the same challenge while placing it in a passage that answers it.
The verse asks who can revive bones after they have decayed. It makes the bodily disappearance in the section’s resurrection example a specific image of bones losing their form.
The answer is that the One who created the bones the first time will revive them. This completes the challenge in 36:78 with the reversal from decay to restoration.

The source section describes words of admonition polishing the heart. This verse says that when God is mentioned hearts tremble and faith increases when His verses are recited, a specific response to heard revelation.

The section’s hadith gloss includes counseling hearts until they are polished. This verse asks whether believers’ hearts have become humble to God’s remembrance and revealed truth, contrasting a softened heart with one that has grown hard.

The source section’s sword and heart-polishing image implies cleansing what has accumulated. This verse says the person who purifies the soul succeeds, giving purification a concrete spiritual outcome.
The next verse says the person who buries or corrupts the soul fails. It supplies the direct opposite of purification and echoes the section’s hidden-versus-brought-into-view boundary.
The same Lord addresses the Prophet and says that He raised his mention. This is a specific public-mention counterpart to the section’s command that the Prophet tell of his Lord’s favor.

The verse says that Moses brought a scripture which people display on pages while concealing much of it. This is a concrete scriptural instance of the section’s movement between what is hidden and what is shown.

The source section defines حديث as speech that reaches a hearer. This verse says the disbelievers will wish the earth were leveled with them but will be unable to conceal any حديث from God, joining speech to the limit of concealment.

The source section says speech received through revelation is called حديث. This verse identifies the recited signs as God’s and asks what discourse people will believe after His signs, tying revelation to a hearer’s response.

The source section defines حديث as speech that reaches people and is then recounted. This verse calls the Quran “this discourse” and addresses the Prophet’s grief if people do not believe it, showing the consequence of a message reaching an unreceptive audience.

On the Day of Judgment, people’s hearing, sight, and skins testify against them. This is a specific reversal of the section’s movement from hidden experience to spoken account: the body itself discloses what its owner concealed.
The people ask their skins why they testified, and the skins answer that God made them speak. This completes 41:20 by naming the source of the disclosure.
The verse says that mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify to what people did. It is a specific image of hidden deeds becoming a spoken record.
The verse says that tongues, hands, and feet will testify to what people did. It repeats the body-as-witness image and makes private actions publicly known.
Each person arrives with a driver and a witness. This verse sets up the judgment scene that continues with the cover removed and sight made sharp in 50:22.
The verse says the written records are spread open. It gives a concrete disclosure of what had been preserved out of sight.
The next verse says each soul will know what it has brought. This completes the opened-record scene with recognition of what was hidden in one’s own deeds.
